contributions.summary: Stratify fungal trait/decomposition regressions by observed temperature and expose fit statistics before model coupling.
Couple woody-fiber loss, multispecies Gause competition, and hyphal extension in one differential state system.
Use a controlled three-species experiment to isolate modeled competition and explain initial-abundance reversal.
Normalize moisture and temperature trait curves into species-specific tolerance factors.
Assemble m_i from a species maximum and two tolerance factors, then hand it to growth, competition, and decomposition interfaces.
Compare short, long, and periodically repeated disturbance scenarios under a shared state model.
Run a five-environment climate panel to compare dominance, persistence, and decomposition.
Compare five-, three-, and two-species decomposition under an equal-total-density intent.
Construct a regional diversity-decrease influence rate from three pairwise fractional losses.
Translate the technical workflow into an introductory biology article with definitions, a game metaphor, result bullets, and a conservation implication.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: Figure 3 supplies isolate-level log extension and log 122-day decomposition observations at 10, 16, and 22 C; Table 1 supplies fitted slopes, intercepts, R-squared values, and p-values.
Reference [7] supplies temperature- and water-potential-conditioned hyphal extension curves for the five named fungi used in Figures 8-10.
Wunderground data provide Columbus hourly September 1-7 and daily September 1-December 31 temperature-humidity histories.
A Santa Fe segment from October 21-November 9 is selected and periodically repeated to construct a 122-day rapid-fluctuation scenario.
One city represents each of five environmental conditions: Santa Fe, Sioux Falls, Columbus, Atlanta, and Codajas.
Tables 3-4 and the implementation prose supply synthetic traits, capacities, fixed 22 C climate, initial densities, initial hyphal length, and a 122-day horizon.
The printed implementation expects custom Get_hyphal_rate and dataprocess modules plus temperature and moisture CSV curve files.
References separate carbon-cycle context, trait/decomposition studies, Gause competition, numerical analysis, weather data, and the water-potential relationship.

independent_extensions.summary: Fit a hierarchical trait-decomposition model with coefficient uncertainty, residual diagnostics, and temperature-moisture interaction rather than two-point intercept interpolation.
Estimate a genuinely pair-specific c_ij matrix from coculture data and test identifiability against the row-constant formulation.
Use bounded, interpolated environmental lookup with unit-tested out-of-range behavior and uncertainty propagation.
Run composition-balanced richness experiments over many species subsets so richness can be separated from species identity.
Compare explicit Euler step sizes, positivity-preserving solvers, and mass-balance residuals before interpreting long-horizon trajectories.
Validate climate-specific density and decomposition outputs against held-out laboratory or field observations rather than internal scenario consistency alone.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: The summary gives a complete four-task route, quantitative headline results, environmental scope, and a bounded assurance close on the first page.
The preprocessing table discloses both coefficient estimates and weak fit statistics, enabling a judge to assess evidence quality quickly.
Equation 1 offers a single inspectable state interface linking the biological mechanisms to the requested decomposition output.
The synthetic baseline provides a readable causal demonstration before the named-species and climate extensions.
Figure 19 aligns climate inputs and density outputs for five conditions in a compact comparison panel.
Exact richness values and three adjacent substrate curves make the diversity comparison easy to audit.
The paper discloses subjective parameters and a two-dimensional response surface instead of hiding them.
The limitations section names interpolation and opponent-invariant competition as concrete improvement targets.

models.summary: Map log extension x to log decomposition y with temperature-specific slope and intercept.
Treat woody-fiber loss as the decomposition amount generated by the modeled fungi.
Decrease V by summed decomposition activity, substrate availability, and a common unused-capacity factor.
Multiply r_i F_i by one minus the sum of coefficient-weighted competitor density fractions.
Scale m_i by the unused fraction of K to produce the hyphal-state derivative.
Construct C with diagonal entries one and repeated c_i across off-diagonal positions in row i.
Set c_i to one minus m_i divided by the sum of all species extension rates.
Replace each derivative with a forward step using the current state and delta t.
Map water condition phi to G(phi) in relation to the maximum of mu_1^i.
Map temperature T to H(T) in relation to the maximum temperature response.
Interpolate the transformed intercept with temperature and apply a shared cross-temperature slope.
Use a linear map from humidity x to water potential w=-5+x/20, formatted to two decimals in code.
Set m_i to m_max^i multiplied by G_i(phi) and H_i(T).
Use the larger of mu_1^i(phi_0) and mu_2^i(T_0) as m_max^i.
Set r_i equal to a shared scaling ratio p times m_i.
Select indexed climate series T_j(t), H_j(t) for Columbus, repeated Santa Fe, and four additional city cases.
Construct richness states S_5, S_3, and S_2 under a fixed total-density rule and compute D_k^j.
Average the 5-to-3, 5-to-2, and 3-to-2 fractional decomposition losses for region i.
Sweep p from 0.05 to 0.3 and n from 50 to 175 for the Columbus 122-day case.
Exponentiate a temperature-derived intercept, multiply hyphal_rate^0.44 and factor, and divide by 100 and 122.
Build r and C from daily m, update F and l, compute D, and update V for 121 steps.

results_trace.summary: low-start-dominance finding: species 3 low initial density -> rapid increase -> outcompetition through high competitiveness. Boundary: Retain the synthetic trait settings, fixed optimal climate, and 122-day horizon.

initial-abundance-reversal finding: species 1 and 2 high initial densities -> competitive pressure -> declining trajectories. Boundary: Initial density alone is not a dominance predictor inside this parameterized system.

residual-coexistence qualifier: highest competitor -> sole winner tendency -> other species persist at low density. Boundary: Use low modeled density rather than extinction unless the state actually reaches the extinction criterion.

efficiency-decline finding: population increase and competition -> lower effective contribution -> declining decomposition efficiency. Boundary: Specify whether the plotted quantity is instantaneous rate, relative contribution, or cumulative loss.
transient-to-balance segmentation: days 0-15 fast decrease -> modeled balance -> days 15-122 slower decrease. Boundary: A visual phase split needs a stated balance criterion if used quantitatively.

thirty-percent plausibility comparison: 122-day substrate trajectory -> about 30 percent mass loss -> source-result comparison. Boundary: Call near agreement a plausibility check, not independent validation, when the same literature informed the model.

Columbus dominance result: lowest initial P.Flavidoalba -> moisture advantage -> visible rise and final dominance. Boundary: Keep Columbus climate, the initial vector, five-species selection, and model assumptions attached.

suppressed-species-reversal possibility: other species brief growth -> low residual amount -> possible dominance after environmental change. Boundary: This is a conditional scenario interpretation, not an observed reversal event.

climate-linked slowing interpretation: steady moisture and decreasing temperature -> slower decomposition -> temperate case narrative. Boundary: Separate what the curve shows from the proposed temperature-and-moisture explanation.

periodic-disturbance experiment: 20-day fluctuating segment -> periodic repetition -> 122-day forced climate. Boundary: Label repetition as a constructed stress scenario rather than recorded long-term weather.

wide-tolerance-dominance result: rapid fluctuation -> high adaptation advantage -> P.Flavidoalba dominance. Boundary: Retain the moderate-to-low temperature range and the authors' higher-temperature caveat.
five-condition transfer experiment: same five fungi -> arid through rainforest climates -> long-term comparison. Boundary: The five chosen city histories bound the environmental panel.

cross-environment-primary-dominance: P.Flavidoalba high modeled competitiveness -> predominance -> radar-profile alignment. Boundary: Radar-chart agreement is internal consistency, not independent evidence.

arid-survival-exception: P.Hartigii low overall competitiveness -> cold and dry tolerance -> arid and semi-arid survival. Boundary: Distinguish persistence from dominance and tie the result to the modeled climate histories.

low-drought-persistence interpretation: M.Tremellosus and H.Setigerum low drought tolerance -> low activity -> modeled survival. Boundary: Treat hiding as metaphor for reduced modeled proliferation, not an implemented behavioral mechanism.

rainforest-competition-reordering: wet-hot climate -> M.Tremellosus and P.Sanguineus advantages -> weakened P.Flavidoalba dominance. Boundary: Preserve the species-specific heat and moisture explanations without inferring a universal ranking.

climate-to-decomposition comparison: five conditions -> seven- and 122-day totals -> higher temperature and moisture associated with higher efficiency. Boundary: Keep the acceptable environmental range and distinguish association in simulations from field causation.

equal-total-density richness ablation: tropical-rainforest baseline -> five, first three, first two species -> 122-day loss. Boundary: Report the retained species and density ratios because richness and composition change together.

exact-richness-result disclosure: D_5^5 63.803 percent -> D_3^5 43.116 percent -> D_2^5 34.110 percent. Boundary: Attach region index, horizon, initial-density control, and percent meaning to the triple.

cross-environment-richness repetition: same richness ablation -> four additional environments -> positive modeled association. Boundary: Repeated simulations across five cases do not remove the species-identity confound.

diversity-decrease influence comparison: three pairwise fractional losses -> averaged influence I^i -> arid 18.405 versus rainforest 33.283 percent. Boundary: Treat I as a constructed model summary and keep the authors' stability interpretation conditional.

weaknesses.summary: Table 4 states multiple-species capacity 200, whereas page 13 prose and the printed code use K=300.
Figure 9 visibly plots water potential against hyphal extension but its caption calls it relative density of woody fibers by time.
Table 2 calls l_i hyphal length yet assigns mm/day, while Equation 1 differentiates l_i again.
Equation 2 presents c_ij notation, but the displayed matrix, coefficient formula, and code use one repeated off-diagonal c_i per row.
The decomposition call already receives a crowding-adjusted hyphal rate and the V update multiplies by the same unused-capacity factor again.
get_hyphal_rate returns moisture factor a to f; temperature affects m but is not passed as a separate factor to f.
Exact float equality for temperature and mapped water potential can fail when climate values do not coincide with CSV grid values.
The custom Get_hyphal_rate and dataprocess modules and both referenced CSV files are not supplied.
Printed code covers the main competitive run and curve plots but omits multi-environment, diversity, sensitivity, and preprocessing workflows.
The richness experiment retains the first species, so reduced richness is confounded with changed species identity and composition.
The sensitivity section infers convergence and robustness from a bounded heatmap without a convergence analysis.
Table 1 R-squared values are 0.4477, 0.3464, and 0.1568 despite small p-values, limiting predictive fit strength.
The prose cites Appendix 7, but the paper has no numbered Appendix 7.
Five selected cities are scenario representatives, not global habitat or field-validation coverage.
